doc.title: Mat Domber interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Learning on private gigs; law school analogy; musicians' pay
summary: Domber says weddings and parties taught young musicians tunes, and compares music school to law school.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well I think that’s — I won’t disagree with what you’re saying — but I can only relate to my individual experience and what you’re talking about is a style and a manner of music that was very, very common years ago. I don’t know how common it is anymore, in reality. You know there were the weddings and the bar mitzvahs and the private parties and such, and a lot of the musicians that I knew and I grew up with, they made a nice living doing that as well as exposing their music in the clubs and places where people could hear them and want to hire them for private events. And that was a very important way also for young musicians to get started in the business because in order to sit in with them they had to learn the tunes, they had to know the proper chord changes, and this was their education. While obviously there is some of that that still goes on, it doesn’t go on in quite the way it used to.

Right. It’s unfortunate because there’s a lot, there’s more also from learning about playing those kinds of gigs, you know how to program a set, how to be professional, how to be comfortable on the stage and talk to people, that whole thing about being a performer you don’t learn in the classroom.

I think that’s very true. Of course it’s always true in any kind of education. I mean take law school for example. Law school doesn’t really prepare you to practice law as such. It doesn’t prepare you for the practicalities of the practice of law. I mean it teaches you how to read a case, it teaches you perhaps how to reason, and it teaches you perhaps about certain substantive facts about different aspects of the law, but it doesn’t really teach you how to practice law. I sort of get the feeling that musical education is somewhat the same

way. I mean it teaches you what the chords are, it teaches you how to play your instrument, it teaches you a little bit about harmony perhaps, teaches you other things that are related, but I don’t really know how well it teaches you how to prepare yourself for the experience of earning money as a musician.
Right. It seems like —you know, the good old days — I guess there used to be more opportunities to make a lousy living than there are now. Now there is fewer opportunities to make a lousy living.

That’s right. That’s right. I mean even, you play here in the clubs, I mean the pay scale is equivalent to what it was forty years ago. It’s very hard for musicians to make a decent living playing, particularly playing jazz. Well of course playing jazz, even in the heyday of swing music, jazz musicians never really made a living.
